humanities_role_explanation: Designed to assess core disciplinary competence in art history and visual reasoning, using curricular materials (Italian secondary-school and US Advanced Placement Art History) verified by professional educators.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Combines text-only questions with multimodal Visual Question Answering (VQA) featuring low-to-medium resolution artwork images accompanying specific items.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Evaluates factual recall of Renaissance art history, artist attribution, stylistic and iconographic reasoning. Tasks are operationalized via seven question formats: single and multiple-choice QA, true/false statement verification, drag-and-drop word positioning, open/closed fill-in-the-blank (cloze completion), and error identification in art-historical texts.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: The benchmark is explicitly scoped to a single domain (Art History/Visual Arts) rather than general-purpose multi-subject evaluation.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates 12 major models across OpenAI (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4 Mini/Nano), Google (Gemini 3.1 Pro/Flash, Gemini 3.5 Flash), Anthropic (Claude Opus/Sonnet 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5), Mistral (Large 3, Pixtral Large), and Qwen (Qwen3-VL-235B).

quantitative_metrics.note: Uses exact match, F1-score (for multi-select and error identification), statement accuracy (for true/false), element accuracy (for positioning), blank accuracy (for completion), and Classical Test Theory parameters (item difficulty and point-biserial discrimination).

summary: The paper introduces EduArt, an educational-level benchmark designed to assess art-historical knowledge and visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs. Constructed from human-authored Italian secondary-school exercises and US AP Art History exams, the benchmark features 871 questions across seven diverse structural formats. Using Classical Test Theory and regression analysis, the authors demonstrate that standard multiple-choice formats fail to distinguish frontier models, whereas alternative generative formats expose major performance drops.
key_findings: Six frontier models achieved near-ceiling performance on multiple-choice items (over 94% accuracy), but their accuracy dropped dramatically on open completion (e.g., Claude Opus 4.6 down to 23.9%) and error identification (e.g., Claude Sonnet 4.6 down to 6.2%). When controlling for other factors, the presence of images actually decreased the likelihood of a correct answer (OR 0.765). Demanding written justifications (motivation condition) improved performance for Anthropic models but degraded performance for Gemini and GPT models.
facets_explanation: The reference answers are directly extracted from official, pre-existing keys for secondary-school textbooks and standardized AP Art History exams. Answering the questions requires retrieving external domain-specific facts, stylistic classifications, and iconographic knowledge not explicitly contained in the visual stimuli or question texts. Because the benchmark uses established educational answer keys graded through programmatic exact or fuzzy string matching, the paper does not address annotator plurality or divergent interpretations.
results_explanation: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieved the highest macro-average score of 82.8% on the 'accuracy' metric under the default answer-only condition (Table 5). The paper reports a large format gap: 'models exceeding 94 percent on multiple choice can fall to 23.9 percent on open completion (Claude Opus 4.6) and 6.2 percent on error identification (Claude Sonnet 4.6)', representing a gap of 88 points (94.3% MCQ minus 6.2% for Claude Sonnet 4.6). A language asymmetry was also reported via logistic regression, with Italian items having significantly lower odds of correct answers ('Language: Italian' OR = 0.459, p < .001, Table 8).
